river.note: Weekly closes since 2023-01-06 (the hub's price cache starts 2022-06); each figure is the trailing four quarters, counted 60 days after the quarter ends (steps); EV/EBITDA uses today's net debt and D&A ratio

epv.note: Price above EPV: the market pays for growth. EPV above tangible book: the business earns more than its assets would cost to rebuild — a sign of a moat (Greenwald). EPV below tangible book: the assets earn less than their cost.

rows.how: the discount rate at which the base-case DCF equals the price

implied_return.note: The yearly return a buyer at today's price earns if each model's assumptions hold (an implied cost of capital). Above the cost of equity: the price leaves room; below: the price already asks for more than the models deliver.

inputs: last four quarters vs the four before (main site revenue history)

an assumption: the hurdle growth investors add to the CAPM rate
an assumption for a forced sale of tangible assets

wacc.formula: WACC = wₑ × kₑ + w_d × k_d × (1 − t);  kₑ = r_f + β × ERP
steps: β (Blume-adjusted) = 0.67 × raw β 0.08 + 0.33 = 0.38  (104 weekly returns vs SPY, R² 0.00)
k_d = 7.10%  (10-year Treasury + 2% (no rate on file)); after tax 7.10% × (1 − 29%) = 5.06%

methods.formula: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC;  EV = Σ FCFF/(1+WACC)^t + TV/(1+WACC)^5;  TV = NOPAT₆ × (1 − g ÷ ROIC) ÷ (WACC − g);  value = (EV − debt + cash − claims) ÷ shares
steps: growth by year 2%, 2%, 2%, 2%, 2%; EBIT margin 11.9%; D&A 2.7% of revenue; capex 6.1%, 5.6%, 5.2%, 4.8%, 4.4% of revenue; ΔWC 10% of each revenue increase
Monte Carlo: 2,000 scenarios, 10th–90th percentile $5.96 – $28.88; P(value > price) = 3%
assumptions: growth σ, margin σ from its own history; WACC ±1 pt; terminal growth 1.5–3%
methods.fit: Operating income is positive ($87.35M over four quarters, revenue growth 2%), so its margins can be projected and its cash flows discounted.

methods.formula: Value per share = peer median P/E × EPS
methods.fit: EPS is positive ($1.27 over four quarters), and 33 peers (SIC 20) have the multiple.

methods.formula: Value per share = (peer median EV/EBITDA × EBITDA − net debt) ÷ shares
methods.fit: EBITDA is positive ($106.9M), and 33 peers (SIC 20) have the multiple.

methods.formula: Value per share = (peer median EV/Sales × Revenue − net debt) ÷ shares
methods.fit: It has revenue ($734.7M over four quarters), and 40 peers (SIC 20) have the multiple.

methods.formula: Value = book + Σ (ROEₜ − kₑ) × Bookₜ₋₁ ÷ (1 + kₑ)ᵗ over 10 years; ROE fades linearly to kₑ; half of earnings retained
methods.fit: Equity is positive ($952.3M) and so is net income ($95.46M), so the return it earns on book value can be compared with what shareholders require.

methods.formula: The same DCF with growth, margin, WACC and terminal growth drawn from what peers did (SIC industry × size) instead of its own history
steps: expected 122.75; 1,000 DCFs with growth, margin, WACC and terminal growth drawn from peers (SIC 20 (Beverages), revenue under $1B, 212 five-year windows)
methods.fit: Its recent revenue growth is 2%. This checks its own DCF against what companies of its industry and size actually achieved, so that optimism in its forecast is caught.

methods.formula: Value per share = owner earnings × (1 + g) ÷ (kₑ − g) ÷ shares; owner earnings = net income + D&A − capex
methods.fit: Owner earnings are positive ($70.53M = net income + D&A − capex), and at the mature stage today's cash earnings are a sound base.

methods.formula: Value per share = (dividends + buybacks) × (1 + g) ÷ (kₑ − g) ÷ shares
methods.fit: It returns cash to shareholders through dividends or buybacks (1.2% of market value a year).

methods.formula: Stage-weighted value = Σ weight × central value of the stage's methods (weights renormalized over the methods available)
steps: 25% × $15.97 (DCF — Monte Carlo 10th–90th percentile) + 20% × $22.23 (Owner earnings capitalized) + 15% × $10.26 (Shareholder yield (dividends + buybacks)) + 25% × $23.81 (P/E vs peers) + 15% × $19.66 (EV/EBITDA vs peers) = $18.88
assumptions: fixed by stage before any result was seen (base_rates.STAGES)
methods.fit: Its stage is “Mature” — revenue growth +1.6% — which fixes these methods and their weights in advance.

assumptions: the Rotation / combined forecasts (forecast ledger, walk-forward)

methods.formula: Graham number = √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share);  22.5 = a P/E of 15 × a P/B of 1.5
assumptions: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor (1949; 1973 edition, ch. 14)
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and book value, the two things Graham asked a defensive investor to pay for — and to pay little for.

methods.formula: Value = EPS × (8.5 + 2g) × 4.4 ÷ Y;  g = expected yearly growth in percent, Y = the AAA corporate yield today
steps: g = 1.6% (its own revenue growth, last four quarters on the four before)
inputs: FRED DAAA (via the Debt & rates module)
assumptions: the P/E of a company that does not grow
the AAA yield when Graham set the formula
an assumption: the formula overstates value at high growth
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and a growth estimate; the formula prices that growth against today's AAA bond yield.

methods.formula: Fair P/E = growth + dividend yield, in percent (5–40);  value = EPS × fair P/E;  PEGY = P/E ÷ (growth + yield)
steps: growth 1.6% (its own revenue growth, last four quarters on the four before); dividend yield 0.9%
today P/E 29.5 → PEGY 11.48 (below 1: cheap for its growth, above 2: dear)
assumptions: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street (1989)
a rule of thumb, not a model of cash flows
0–35%; its own revenue growth, last four quarters on the four before
analysts look one or two years ahead; Lynch meant several
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and a growth rate, so its P/E can be set against the growth and yield it delivers.

methods.formula: Net current asset value per share = (current assets − total liabilities − other claims) ÷ shares;  a net-net trades below two-thirds of it
inputs: frames: total assets − equity − other claims
assumptions: Fixed assets, goodwill, the business itself
Graham, Security Analysis (1934): a liquidation floor
methods.fit: Its current assets and liabilities are on file. Net-nets are rare among large companies; a positive figure is a floor that ignores everything the business owns beyond working capital.

methods.formula: EPV = adjusted earnings ÷ WACC − net debt;  adjusted earnings = normalized EBIT × (1 − t) + D&A − maintenance capex;  normalized EBIT = average margin × revenue
steps: normalized EBIT = 11.9% × $734.7M = $87.35M  (the last four quarters' EBIT margin (fewer than three years on file))
maintenance capex = $40.51M  (capex $44.51M − growth capex (PP&E $247.4M ÷ revenue × revenue gain $11.89M = $4.00M))
assumptions: the business as it is, forever
methods.fit: It earns an operating profit over the cycle; EPV values that profit as if it never grew, which shows how much of the price is a bet on growth.

methods.formula: FCFE = net income − (1 − d) × (capex − D&A + ΔWC);  value = Σ FCFE ÷ (1 + kₑ)ᵗ + terminal ÷ (1 + kₑ)⁵;  terminal = net income₆ × (1 − g ÷ ROE) ÷ (kₑ − g)
steps: net margin 13.0%; d (debt share of capital) = 0%; growth 2%, 2%, 2%, 2%, 2%
assumptions: its own growth fading to terminal
methods.fit: It is profitable with positive equity, so the cash left for shareholders after reinvestment and borrowing can be projected.

methods.formula: ln(EV/Sales) = a + b₁ × growth + b₂ × ln(operating margin, at least 0.5%) + b₃ × loss flag + b₄ × ln(revenue, $B) + sector effect;  value = (fitted EV/Sales × revenue − net debt) ÷ shares
inputs: last four quarters vs the four before
assumptions: every covered non-financial company with revenue ≥ $50M, today; ridge λ = 1
methods.fit: It is a non-financial company with revenue on file, so the multiple the market pays companies with its growth, margin, size and sector applies.

methods.formula: Value = D₀ × [(1 + g_L) + H × (g_S − g_L)] ÷ (kₑ − g_L);  growth falls in a straight line from g_S to g_L over 2H years
assumptions: an assumption: dividends rarely grow faster for a decade
methods.fit: It pays a dividend whose growth is likely to slow from today's pace to the economy's, which the H-model spreads over ten years.
